newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's stocks fall on fears of labour unrest.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's stocks fall on fears of labour unrest.

text.p: South Korean stocks fell to their lowest level in 38 months on Thursday as government proposals to revise labour laws ignited already growing anger among unions that plan token strikes next week.
"The spectre of violent labour strife seems to be reviving. It's scaring investors away from the market," said Choo Hee-yup, a broker at Dongwon Securities.

Since the labour reform plans, the first in 43 years, were announced on Tuesday, unions have complained that the emphasis is on helping business and making it more competitive, not protecting workers rights.
Unions object in particular to articles that open the way to worker layoffs and the introduction of flexible working hours, which would hit seasonal workers and overstaffed industries.

The country's two biggest umbrella union groups stepped up their sabre-rattling on Thursday, announcing plans for mainly token strikes over the next two weeks when the reforms are likely to be debated and passed by parliament before it goes into recess on December 19.
"We are planning a token strike next week," said an official of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions. "It will be followed by an allout strike unless our demands are met."

The confederation, South Korea's second largest labour group, said its members represented major workplaces, including Hyundai Motor Co, the country's largest car maker, Kia Motors Corp, Hyundai Heavy Industries Co and Daewoo Heavy Industries Co.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the nation's largest union organisation, said it planned a one-hour stike on December 16 and a longer stoppage on December 19.
"We will work out follow-up steps after watching the results," said a federation official.

Brokers said a large-scale strike would be a drastic blow to an already staggering stock market. On Thursday, the market lost 9.57 points to end at 706.30, its lowest since September 25, 1993, when it closed at 703.55.

"Even without a strike, the index could fall to the 680 level this year because of weakening fundamentals. I cannot possibly imagine the consequence of labour unrest," said Yoo Jae-kyong, a broker at Daishin Securities.

Brokers said the banking industry, long regarded as overstaffed, may be the most vulnerable to labour unrest in the near term because the reforms would allow companies to lay off workers for economic reasons.
"Banks are most vulnerable to the reforms because of possible merger and aquisition deals as the industry opens wider to foreign competition," said Lee Young-won, a broker at Daewoo Securities.
Kim Joon-il, an economist at the Korea Development Institute, agreed that South Korea's financial sector was the most over-employed and backward in the country.
"Companies need to secure flexibility in employment. That is one of the most important tasks to do in order to improve industrial competitiveness," Kim said.
